correctness.rationale: Two fixed parts of sum s leave floor((n-s)/2) unordered completions when n-s>=2. For n>=30 the largest size exceeds 13, and sums 2 and (only at odd n) 3 are the sole maximal centers. The canonical occurrence labels encode multiset intersections, and a triple of labels can occur in at most one partition because it forces the remaining part. Thus distinct compatible partitions meet in exactly two labels. For a nontrivial family choose such a pair with common labels I and disjoint remainders A,B of size two, and a third member not containing I. Members containing I must pick at least one external label from this third member (at most four triple completions); members containing one label of I must pick one each from A and B (at most eight); those avoiding I must equal A union B (at most one). This proves the uniform cap and forces full stars at n>=30. I inspected both supplied graph searches and outputs, without running the uploaded code. The independent interval-cut/submultiset implementation /workspace/branches/partition_fixed_check.py was actually run: target clique exists and target+1 does not for each n=4..29, using only induced minimum-degree pruning and exhaustive include/exclude branching. It reproduced all 26 exact maxima, including 4 on the six vertices at n=9. The bounded run does not certify other k,t or classify small-order extremizers.

evidence: Borg proves star optimality at n<=2k-t+1 and n>=3tk^5, i.e. n<=7 and n>=6144 for these parameters. The theorem's uniqueness clause needs k>=t+3, and Remark 1.9 already gives the tied odd-order center. Person–Schweser's sufficiently-large-k regime does not establish a result for k=4; their counterexample hypothesis t<=ceil(k/4) also fails here.
